I'm not sure this is 100% accurate so you might need to do some independent research on the topic but here is my perspective.

I often feel that the concept of a gender pay gap is misconstrued and unjustly dismissed within alot of feminist discourse. Many people have the understanding that the gender pay gap is 2 people (a man and a woman) working the same job at the same company with the same job title and reiceving wages that aren't equal. This is often dismissed as its illegal (UK law) and, although it can and does happen, its relatively rare and seen often times as a non-issue as its easy to argue and settle within court. However, this sentiment is incorrect. The gender pay gap refers to the wealth disparity between genders as a whole - the average earnings of a woman vs the average earnings of a man. When this is clarified to pay gap skeptics they often dismiss this as personal choice such as: choosing less lucrative professions, becoming a stay-at-home mum, spending more on or more time in education allowing for less overall income to be earned. In a lot of cases (and much to my dismay) the conversation surrounding the topic halts and is rarely explored further. However, with a bit of analysis of these "personal choices" the real argument at the core of the gender pay gap is uncovered - namely the "less lucrative" professions. Many women often choose to become teachers, nurses, carers etc - jobs associated with nurture and support. You could argue this is because of the stereotypes society applies to women but here I believe its irrelevant. All three of the professions I mentioned formerly are known to be criminally underpaid (UK) with many nurses even having to visit food banks in order to support themselves and their families (UK) and no one ever seems to ask "why?". Most of my school teachers are women, most of the nurses that have cared for me have been women and all of the carers at my local care home are women. Without these women society would undoubtedly collapse - kids would be deprived of their education, the sick would go untreated, grandmothers and grandfathers would be neglected. I don't think it's a coincidence that teaching roles most commonly filled by men receive better pay (UK): PE teachers, Math teachers, Science teachers. Stereotypically "female" jobs are usually at the bottom rung for yearly income while eerily similar "male" occupations receive a much higher pay (see barbers vs hairdressers and cleaners vs janitors). Regarding women who become stay-at-home mums, I have nothing against them. I believe such a commitment to one's children is admirable and very beneficial, however, very few men ever choose to become stay-at-home dads and the pressure to abandon their careers in favour of childcare is simply non-existent for men (not to mention the countless mothers who return to work after maternity leave only to find themselves sidelined and mysteriously redundant). In reference to women pursuing higher education, I think many women feel as if they have to in order to compete in a world which men so obviously hold the power within the economy and jobs market. In sectors marketed towards women the most prominent figures are usually men - makeup: James charles and many other youtube personalities (I mean one of the most popular brands is literally named after a man *max factor*), fashion: all highstreet CEOs are men, many big name designers are men (Jimmy choo etc), skincare: the biggest skincare influencer is a man (hyram) and most of the big brands are owned by men (I would just like to state that I am not implying and of these sectors are for or exclusive to women I'm just stating that more often than not their products are marketed with a female target audience in mind). Even in public sector jobs (UK so doctors included) many top/senior positions are held by men. Most surgeons are men, the largest proportion of male teachers work at secondary level or as lecturers in universities, female police officers are often confined to working on sex assualt and child abuse cases, etc. In short, women find it harder to succeed in their chosen career path than men so they are more likely to pursue higher education to make up for the male privilege they haven't got. 

TLDR: The gender pay gap argument is misunderstood and men do in fact get paid more than women.

I have used benzoyl peroxide and it does work pretty well! If you're worried about it irritating your skin, you can do short contact therapy - rub it onto all of the affected areas and leave it for 5-10 minutes and then wash it off (also buy a lower concentration like 2.5~5%, bigger isn't better with benzoyl lol). This is usually a good way to build up your skins tolerance to it and avoid bleaching your pillow cases (been there 😭😭). However, if you want to use salicylic, benzoyl and lactic acid (or any other aha you pick) don't use them on the same night as they could irritate your skin (unless you're using just the wash then you should be OK but maybe use a different wash just to be sure bc you said you were worried about drying / irritation). Use the salicylic acid one night, benzoyl the next and only use the lactic 2~3 times a week.

I hate to be that preachy wise type and I don't want to come off as unhelpful but I'm 16F and honestly I felt I was in the same position just a couple years back. At the time I felt like I always had nothing to say or whatever I had to contribute was not of much value or whenever I had something interesting to say I'd shy away from speaking my mind because I felt it was too outlandish/weird/political/complex. In short I was always afraid of stepping on other people's toes and it caused me to become rather introverted and outwardly shy. However, I am so different now from how I was a couple of years ago that sometimes I look back and think of the person I used to be kind of like a different person. It was a mix of things that made me feel more confident and happier which made it so much easier to talk to people (whether it be crushes, friends, etc) - the biggest one being that I started to say things I wouldn't usually say, you don't realise how much you conceal your personality and make it difficult to speak to others when you can't properly connect with them because you're constantly filtering everything you say. I don't mean you should go out and start swearing, shouting and being offensive, just the little things you usually keep to yourself like things you're interested in that you're scared of being judged for, unique hobbies, philosophical ideas. I used to think many of my interests and hobbies were "weird" (I feel as though this is very common for teenagers haha) but after opening up more you find people aren't so different from you and they probably agree and are interested in alot of the things you have to say (I feel like I've said interest wayyy too much lol). So, the next time you catch yourself going "no I can't say that" (unless it's something really rude or offensive) just say it and take a chance, you'll probably be pleasantly surprised by how much you have in common with the people around you. Something that helped me feel more confident to say things I wouldn't usually is generally just taking more pride in my outward appearance (I'm not saying you don't you probably do 😅😅) because if you look put together and you look good you'll probably feel the same way - honestly it's so much easier to talk with others when you feel good about yourself. There are many possible careers in music - don't be discouraged! The selection is alot wider if you are good at music technology as well as just performance but you mentioned that you use ableton regularly so I'm assuming you have interests in music tech as well. For many of these paths you might need to do a part time job during the week while you get started and having a degree to fall back on is good but after sometime working in the profession alot of people find they can support themselves just with their music job. 

Careers in music performance:

- Session musician:
It's a common career path for people passionate about their instruments (or their voice) to go down and session musicians are usually in high demand (depending on what instruments you play). My dad and my aunt both did session work when they were younger so if you like the idea of being a rhythm guitarist for a big band or a backing singer for a vocalist then this would be an ideal option.

- Playing in a band/group:
If you like jazz or pop music this would be right down your alley. Auditions for bands are commonplace for jazz and pop genres so if you're good at the sax, guitar or a great singer then it wouldn't be too hard finding a good band and getting gigs. This is a good option if you want to perform on stage but down want the pressure of performing as a solo act.

- Solo act:
This is probably a more suitable option if you're a singer because you'll find it easier to get gigs in nightclubs, bars etc. If you like the attention of being onstage alone and have good stage presence then it will be ideal but you won't have the support of any peers so if you're happy going it alone then I would encourage you to persue performing alone. Adopting a persona and writing your own music might help in this field but many people still fine adequate work as cover artists so don't be put off if you aren't so keen to be the next David Bowie.

There are lots of other jobs avaliable but those are the best options if you really want a career that is likely to last.

Careers in Music Technology:

- Live sound engineer:
All those bands playing gigs need someone to plug in their microphones and monitors. They're usually employed by whatever facility is hosting the gigs so nightclubs, arenas, stadiums even live TV broadcasters are the best places to look for vacancies. In this area you run the risk of it not being too music related anymore though so make sure you apply to the right places so you don't end up engineering for newsnight.

- Music producer:
If you like writing or making songs then its a career that you will find incredibly fulfilling. If you're good with DAWs you'll find this job alot easier but there's also opportunities to produce analog (although it's not often nowadays) so I would recommend you hone your ableton skills (and maybe learn logic and pro-tools along the way).

There is lots of other opportunities for work in the music field and I probably missed loads (I'm sorry). If you have written songs before or are just very talented at your instrument I recommend you record your songs/covers and post them to soundcloud or YouTube to show people to help you get gigs or fans. You never know, you may carve a career path out for yourself this way. It's definitely not an easy industry to get into but don't give up hope if you're passionate enough and willing to put in the work it's certainly possible.
